accuracy.evidence: Covers all three evidence statements of the topic: describing a noticed pattern as a general rule in words (any number add 0 stays the same, the exact example in the topic), testing the rule on unseen cases including large numbers (1000 + 26, 120 + 64), and the difference between noticing and proving (odd + odd shown by pairing the two spare dots). The fixed multiplication rule (a number above 0 times more than 1 gets bigger) is mathematically correct for all the listed cases.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the errors 8-9 year olds make when generalising: stating one example as a rule ('3 + 0 = 3', prediction step 1 and challenge 'one'), vague rules ('Numbers are fun'), stopping after the examples you started with, treating a rule as a vote of many fits against one breaker ('9 beats 1'), throwing a rule away instead of adding a condition, and thinking 50 examples prove it.

lab_distinct.evidence: Distinct from the Spotting Patterns lab, which continues repeating shapes, finds number sequence rules and adds -ed to words: here learners assemble a three-part rule sentence from tiles, test a fixed rule on new sums, hunt for counterexamples to a claim, toggle conditions while a live case table shows fits, breaks and not covered, and drag dot leftovers together to see a proof.

lab_teaches.evidence: Steps follow the scientific cycle for rules: state it precisely, test it on unseen and extreme cases, actively look for a breaker, repair the rule with conditions until the live table shows no breaks, then ask why it must hold. Each completion message names the general idea, not just the answer.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions are committed before the action: whether '3 + 0 = 3' is a rule or one example, whether a single example can overturn a claim that fitted twice, and whether 50 tested odd + odd sums prove the rule for every number. Each reveal links the prediction to what the learner then sees in the lab.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven challenge kinds (rule versus example, next test, find a breaker, one breaker against many fits, fixing a rule, what makes a proof, why odd + odd is even) with eight tailored feedback messages, so a learner who says '9 beats 1' is told a rule is not a vote, and one who picks 'more examples' learns that only a reason shows it always works.

readability.evidence: Kid explanation FK grade 1.1 with short sentences and concrete numbers; adult explanation FK 6.1, both inside the family audience limits. Mathematical words (rule, breaker, condition, proof) are each introduced with a plain example before being used in questions.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries an example, a test or a reason. The family tip is a specific dinner-table game (say a rule, others hunt for a breaker, then fix it together) that rehearses the lesson's exact cycle rather than general praise.

mobile.evidence: Playwright walkthrough on iPhone 13 completed all six steps and five tasks with no console errors. Screenshots at 390 px show the rule tiles, case grid, multiplier grid, condition table and dot pairs fully visible; labels use max width so nothing clips, and every tile has a large button twin.

accessibility.evidence: axe reported zero violations in dark and light themes on desktop and phone. The canvas carries a live aria-label with the current state, each canvas tile is mirrored by a labelled HTML button (including 'Join the leftovers' for the drag), and colour is never the only cue because each case also says fits, breaks it or not covered.
